title: Why a peak is strong, weak or absent
key_message: Only a vibration that makes the charge oscillate absorbs: C=O is very strong, symmetric CO₂ is invisible.
body: Infrared light «pushes» electric charges. If a vibration makes the distribution of charge oscillate, it absorbs; if not, it is invisible. The C=O group has very different charges on its two atoms: it gives very strong peaks. In CO₂ the symmetric stretch changes nothing in the charge: it is not seen.
The figure shows the modes of CO₂ and water: the arrow is the oscillating [[dipole-moment|dipole]].
for_chemists: [[selection-rule|Selection rule]]: a mode is IR-active if the dipole moment changes along the coordinate (∂μ/∂Q ≠ 0); the intensity grows with (∂μ/∂Q)². A permanent dipole is not needed: the asymmetric stretch of CO₂ is active. N₂ and O₂ do not absorb. In the harmonic oscillator Δv = ±1; with [[anharmonicity|anharmonicity]] Δv = ±2, ±3 are possible too, weakly.

CO₂ (linear, 3N−5 = 4 modes): νas 2349 and the bend 667 (doubly degenerate) absorb; νs is IR-inactive (Raman, Fermi dyad 1285/1388). H₂O (3N−6 = 3 modes): all active, in the gas phase 3656.7 (νs), 1594.6 (δ), 3755.8 (νas) cm⁻¹. A symmetric alkene C=C may not be seen.
In the figure the geometry, partial charges and amplitudes are illustrative, not calculated: they show whether the dipole changes, not by how much.

figure.alt: A vibrating CO₂ or water molecule; below it an arrow shows the change of the dipole and a small plot shows the dipole over time.
figure.caption: The oscillating dipole: only the modes in which it changes absorb infrared.
